summary:
Portugal remains among the safer European destinations for transgender visitors, standing under the national framework of the Portuguese Republic. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change currently runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which allows self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offending. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an offence determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated, with aggravated assault punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carrying one to eight years' imprisonment.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th at 67%, down one place, with no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban. A new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children.

On 20 March 2026 the Portuguese Parliament approved bills from PSD, Chega and CDS-PP that reverse the gender-identity law, the first legislative vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition. The proposals passed 124 to 79 and were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees, directly targeting the 2018 self-identification law. At first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform.

IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal issued a joint statement warning that the three bills debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition, and that if adopted Portugal would lose at least four Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France. The psychologists' order and trans groups called the rollback a 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Hundreds protested outside the Assembly against the bills.

A separate set of three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 by a 151-79 vote would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula. Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality warns the bills worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties.

Justice Ministry data show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon, even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 law scrapped. European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 questions the Commission on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.

The Provedoria da Justica, Portugal's Ombudsman, has requested constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which establishes the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, questioning the hate-speech provision itself. Portugal's Parliament formally adopted 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia in 2015.
tangentialFactors:
Portugal's standing is regressing relative to European peers. ILGA-Europe's joint statement projects that adoption of the three bills would drop Portugal at least four Rainbow Map places, below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France, reversing its status as a European reference point on trans rights.

The rollback has generated sustained public contestation: hundreds protested outside the Assembly of the Republic in March 2026, the Order of Psychologists and trans organisations denounced the bills, and socialist deputies invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman beaten and killed by youths in Porto, drawing a hostile response from Chega's Hugo Soares.

Annual pride parades in Lisbon and Porto attract thousands of participants and spectators, and Lisbon hosts Queer Lisboa, one of Europe's largest LGBT film festivals, indicating a visible and established community infrastructure alongside the legislative turbulence.

Portugal has a documented history of external correction on LGBT rights: in 1999 the European Court of Human Rights fined the country after a domestic court made homophobic statements in ruling against a gay father's custody of his daughter, ordering custody returned to him.

Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties and assesses a Bloco de Esquerda bill as compatible with school human-rights obligations.

outOfScopeNotes:
The three roll-back bills had completed first reading and committee referral as of the latest sourced reporting (March to August 2026); whether they have been enacted into law, and in what final form, is unresolved in the available sources.

The precise scope of the proposed mandatory medical opinion, including which practitioners could certify and whether a waiting period or sterilisation-type condition attaches, is not specified in the inventory and remains unresolved.

ILGA-Europe's projected loss of at least four Rainbow Map places assumes full adoption of the bills; the actual 2027 Rainbow Map score under any enacted or amended version is not sourced.

The outcome of the Provedoria da Justica's request for constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement practice for the Penal Code's aggravated-offence provisions and Article 176-C in reported cases against trans victims is not documented in the inventory.
